children: At the BW Sustainable World Conclave, Deepak Thakur highlights credibility, empowerment, and ecosystem-building as businesses pursue rapid sustainable growth

At the 9th Annual BW Sustainable World Conclave & Awards 2026, Deepak Thakur, MD & CEO, Hinduja Renewables, said sustainable growth requires organisations to scale their leadership, credibility and ecosystems alongside ambition. Speaking at the closing keynote on 17 September, Thakur explored what happens when business ambitions move faster than the systems needed to support them.
Scaling Beyond The Numbers

Thakur said the increasing focus on scale — from customers and factories to investments and renewable energy capacity — needs to be accompanied by a closer examination of what organisations risk losing as they grow.
“Your strengths scale, but your weaknesses grow exponentially too,” he said, pointing to how weak processes, poor decisions and small compromises can become embedded in an organisation as it expands.

For Thakur, credibility is one of the first qualities tested by rapid growth. Recalling a competitive renewable energy bidding process, he described how his team stopped bidding after the tariff crossed the threshold approved by the investment committee, despite months of preparation and the disappointment of losing the project.

While the organisation later won another bid, Thakur said the earlier loss was more significant in establishing credibility because the team demonstrated that it would adhere to its principles under pressure.
He said credibility must extend beyond senior leadership to engineers, procurement managers, project leaders and sales teams.“Culture is what people choose when they can choose otherwise,” he said.

Thakur also cited McKinsey research covering around 50 Indian companies and 80,000 employees, which, according to him, found that healthier organisations delivered three times the long-term shareholder value of less healthy organisations.
Empowering Leadership

As businesses grow, Thakur said leaders must avoid becoming the central point for every decision, conflict and exception. Instead, organisations need to develop people faster than they develop dependency on individual leaders.

Drawing on an early experience at Thermax, where he was asked to move from corporate planning and strategy to lead a call centre, Thakur said leadership also involves recognising potential in people before they recognise it themselves.
He described this as creating a multiplier effect, where one leader develops five people, those five develop 50, and the process continues across the organisation.

Thakur linked this to the concept of “structured empowerment”, arguing that empowerment without structure can lead to chaos, while structure without empowerment can create bureaucracy. For organisations scaling rapidly, he advocated holding purpose tightly while allowing flexibility in methods, ideas and solutions.
Building The Ecosystem

Thakur said the challenge becomes more complex when an organisation is ready to scale but the surrounding ecosystem is not. Renewable energy developers may be able to build generation capacity faster than evacuation infrastructure can develop, while EV manufacturers can scale production faster than charging networks. Similarly, commitments to circularity can move faster than recycling and traceability systems.

He argued that organisations cannot simply treat these gaps as someone else’s problem when they directly affect their mission. However, this does not mean companies should attempt to own every part of the ecosystem.

“Sometimes we must build what is missing, sometimes we should partner with others who can do it better,” he said, adding that sustainable ecosystems may require several stakeholders to create the conditions for growth.

Thakur concluded by returning to the question his daughter asked him 18 years ago about what he could do about climate change. For him, the question has evolved into a broader leadership challenge: when a problem is larger than an organisation but it can influence part of it, leaders must focus on creating the conditions for progress rather than waiting for the ecosystem to become ready.
Mahek Asghar
BW Reporters The author is a trainee correspondent at BW Businessworld.
